summary:
LC-41: The Last Lifeline is a retro browser game where players design, fly and rescue Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object.

Players first act as the 1977 mission team. They choose an objective, rocket, launch window, nuclear power (RTGs), fuel, ten real instruments and an antenna, while live meters show how each choice trades mass, power, budget, data and lifetime. The game blocks a launch that is too heavy, underpowered or over budget, and explains why. Then they fly the real Grand Tour: photographing Jupiter, steering a burn at Saturn, finding the Pale Blue Dot, and keeping the probe alive as its power fades through real events up to the one-light-day milestone on 18 November 2026. When the real story ends, a what-if timeline begins in which Voyager wakes up and mines an asteroid to survive.

Up to four players can share one screen as Flight Director, Engineer, Science Officer and CAPCOM, each with competing goals. A mission report explains why the mission succeeded or failed. LC-41 makes mission trade-offs something students feel, not just read about.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LC-41: The Last Lifeline is a retro browser game about designing and flying Voyager 1. It has three parts:

1. Mission design (1977): six short steps. Pick an objective, a launch vehicle (Atlas-Centaur or Titan IIIE-Centaur), a launch window, the spacecraft body, the number of RTGs, the hydrazine load, ten real Voyager instruments, an antenna dish and a tape recorder. A live pixel spacecraft is built as you choose, and meters show mass, power, budget, data, lifetime and science. Launch is blocked if the spacecraft is too heavy for the rocket, short on power or over budget, and the game explains why.

2. The real mission: photograph Jupiter's moons within a data budget, fly a trajectory-correction burn at Saturn, vote on Titan or Pluto, find the Pale Blue Dot, then manage power through the "Long Night" as the RTGs fade, through real events: the termination shock, the heliopause, the 2023 memory fault, the February 2026 power drop and the one-light-day milestone on 18 November 2026.

3. A what-if timeline: when power runs out, Voyager wakes up as an artificial lifeform, sends a drone through a debris field to mine an asteroid, docks, restores its power and points its antenna home.

A mission report then scores the run, gives star ratings and explains in plain language why it succeeded or failed.

HOW IT WORKS

A simple physical model drives every consequence. RTG power decays from about 470 W in 1977 to about 220 W in 2026 (about 4 W lost per year now), data capacity scales with dish area, fuel is spent by burns and by pointing, and the design choices carry through the whole flight. A small dish loses data at Jupiter, too little hydrazine loses Earth-pointing early, and fewer RTGs end the mission years sooner.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students rarely get to try a whole mission from concept to operation. LC-41 lets them feel the trade-offs instead of reading about them: payload capacity, power budgets, launch windows, data rates and fault protection are all learned by playing. There is no single right design, so players experiment, fail safely and try again. It runs in any browser with no install, so a classroom can play it instantly.

COLLABORATION

Two to four players share one screen as Flight Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Officer and CAPCOM. Each owns part of the design and has a personal goal (stay under budget, keep spare power, fly more instruments, lose less data) that pulls against the others, so they have to negotiate. Big decisions go to a vote.

CREATIVITY

It is a real mission told as a game, with a twist: after the true story ends, it becomes science fiction, clearly labelled as fiction. Chiptune music, combos, lightning bonuses on Jupiter, surprise emergencies (solar flares, micrometeoroids, bit-flips), radio chatter and a hall of fame keep it fun.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Accuracy: real events and values, simplified for play, with a real-vs-fiction timeline in the game. Accessibility: step-by-step design, a how-to-play card before every mini-game, keyboard, mouse and touch controls, and four difficulty levels including Sandbox. Reliability: tested with dozens of automated full playthroughs, extreme designs and a failsafe retry for every mini-game.

TOOLS

HTML5 Canvas, JavaScript, CSS and the Web Audio API (music and sound generated in code), with no frameworks or server. Hosted on GitHub Pages.
